learning: Iteration 0 showed all runs leaving the track with max_error about 0.06-0.07 m and one line-loss event each. Narrowing the track raises yaw gain by about 20 percent for the same kp, so kp was scaled to hold effective gain steady. Next race should show whether max_error drops below 0.06 m and whether steering_oscillation rises on the slalom.
notes: Drivetrain-test package: the Builder's narrower, lighter body (track 0.10 m, mass 0.6 kg) with kp scaled down to 1.25 to offset the higher yaw gain, kd raised to 0.25 for damping, and base_speed trimmed to 1.5. Sensor row and line recovery are unchanged from iteration 0 so the effect of the drivetrain change can be isolated.
rationale: Iteration 0 (the baseline, kp 1.5, kd 0.15, wheel_track 0.12, mass 0.8) left all 60 trials off track at 11-16% progress. max_error was 0.061-0.070 m against the 0.060 m limit, and each run had exactly one line-loss event, so the robot drifted off the line rather than losing sight of it early. The Builder's max_error 0.06 limit cannot be raised by body width (0.18 m gives 0.0575 m), so the robot's error must come down. The Builder's test changes only the drivetrain: wheel_track 0.12 to 0.10 m and mass 0.8 to 0.6 kg. Turn rate per unit of turn command scales as 1/wheel_track, so the effective steering gain rises by about 20 percent. Keeping kp at 1.5 would risk overcorrection and oscillation, so I scale kp down to 1.25 to hold the effective gain near the baseline. The lighter robot has less yaw inertia, so the response is quicker and needs slightly more damping. I raise kd from 0.15 to 0.25. ki stays at 0 because the integral adds lag and the motor mismatch is small. base_speed drops from 1.6 to 1.5 to reduce the lateral speed at bends while keeping close to the 1.5 m/s average the 3 s limit needs. The sensor weights, line_loss mode and sensor row are unchanged so the drivetrain effect can be read cleanly. I expect max_error to fall below 0.06 m on the oval and s-bend, with a risk of more steering oscillation on the slalom.
